4. Final remarks
The basic framework of the requirements for set-off, as explained above, is not fundamentally changed by the revision of
the JCC in 2017. The provisions amended by the revision are as follows:
The previous provision concerning the manifestation of intention to limit a set-off has referred only to a bona fide third
party regardless of gross negligence (JCC prev. Art. 505 (2)). In contrast, according to the current provision, when a third
party is grossly negligent, even if they don’t know the limitation of set-off, it may be duly asserted against them (JCC Art.
505 (2))86.
JCC prohibited any set-off of claims arising from tortious acts (JCC prev. Art. 509). This rule, even when considered in
light of its underlying rationale, excessively and unnecessarily deprived creditors of the opportunity to exercise set-off.

Charles Ho Wang Mak
University of Bristol School of Law, Bristol, England, UK
This article offers a valuable and much-needed account of Japanese set-off law in English.
It provides a comprehensive overview of the requirements for set-off under Japanese law, a topic
that has not been extensively discussed in international literature. In particular, the article's
systematic breakdown of set-off into affirmative and negative requirements is excellent. Your use
of specific examples and clear explanations of concepts like "Sousai-Tekijou" (eligibility for set-off)
and the distinction between active and passive claims makes the complex topic approachable. The
section on set-off in bankruptcy proceedings is also particularly strong.
However, you should consider a few key improvements:
1. While the abstract provides a good overview, a formal introduction would set the stage,
state the paper's aim, and highlight its contribution to the English-language literature.
2. Your response acknowledges that some passages are difficult to translate directly from
Japanese legal texts. I suggest a collaborative effort with a native English speaker with a
legal background to smooth out these parts. The goal is not to change the meaning but to
improve readability for an international audience. Specific sections that could benefit from
this include the third paragraph under 1-1-2 and the first paragraph under 3-4-2.
3. While you intentionally avoided a full comparative study for the sake of conciseness, a brief,
well-structured section in the main body (not just the conclusion) could address the German
and French law comparisons. This could also be an opportunity to clarify or revise
statements, such as the one about German law's stance on knowledge of assignment (BGB
Art. 392 and 406).
4. If possible, the complexity of set-off, especially in a tripartite relationship or in bankruptcy,
would be significantly easier to understand with a few simple diagrams. These visuals could
illustrate the flow of claims and the impact of concepts like attachment and assignment.

Rebecca Parry
Nottingham Trent University, Nottingham, UK
This article provides a systematic doctrinal discussion of set-off under Japanese law. Since this is
an area of law that attracts limited discussion internationally this will be an important account,
covering key statutes and case law. It will be helpful for anyone who is aiming to understand the
operation of set-off both in insolvency and outside of it in Japan.
In terms of readability, an introduction should be added to explain to the reader the aim of the
paper. This can be used to highlight the important laws and what has influenced their
development. Also to highlight the contribution that this article makes to the literature. I believe
that it is the only recent source that will discuss set-off under Japanese law in English.
The article includes a good number of references. It is good practice to indicate where texts are in
the Japanese language and to give the Japanese titles.
The material would have been enhanced with a greater comparative element but is still valuable
for the reasons already given.
